words.definition: Marked by a strong, often controversial bias in favor of a particular cause.
words.example: The documentary was so tendentious that it felt like campaign propaganda rather than reporting.
words.mnemonic: It TENDS toward one side — a 'tendency' baked right into the word.

words.definition: To win someone over, through reasoning or appeal, to a view or action.
words.example: She finally persuaded her cautious parents to let her travel alone.
words.mnemonic: per- (through) + suade (suave, sweet talk): sweet-talk someone all the way through to your side.

words.definition: To talk someone out of a course of action, often by warning of consequences.
words.example: His mentor tried to dissuade him from quitting just weeks before graduation.
words.mnemonic: dis- (away) + suade (sweet talk): sweet-talk someone AWAY from what they planned.

words.definition: To urge someone earnestly and forcefully to do something.
words.example: The coach exhorted his players to leave everything on the field in the final quarter.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'egg-zort' — picture someone egging you on, shouting to spur you into action.

words.definition: A long, tedious piece of writing or speech, usually an angry rant.
words.example: He posted a rambling screed attacking everyone who had ever disagreed with him.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'screech' — a long written screech of grievances that never stops.

words.definition: To state something firmly and confidently as being true.
words.example: She asserted her innocence again and again, refusing to waver from her story.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'a-certain' inside it — you put something forward as certain.

words.definition: To put an idea or assumption forward as a starting point for reasoning.
words.example: The philosopher posited that free will might be nothing more than a comforting illusion.
words.mnemonic: Short for 'position' — you set an idea down in position on the table.

words.definition: To offer a theory or proposal for others to consider.
words.example: At the conference she propounded a bold new theory of how memory decays.
words.mnemonic: pro- (forward) + pound: you POUND an idea forward for the room to weigh.

words.definition: To bring forward facts or examples as proof in an argument.
words.example: The lawyer adduced three eyewitnesses to support her client's alibi.
words.mnemonic: ad- (toward) + duce (to lead, as in 'produce'): you LEAD evidence toward your point.

words.definition: To strengthen or give support to something, such as an argument or morale.
words.example: Strong quarterly sales bolstered the CEO's case for a rapid expansion.
words.mnemonic: A bolster is a long firm pillow that props you up — so to bolster is to prop up.

words.definition: To prop up or reinforce something, physically or with evidence.
words.example: He buttressed his thesis with data drawn from a dozen independent studies.
words.mnemonic: A flying buttress is the stone arm that holds up a cathedral wall — support made visible.

words.definition: To make something stronger or more secure against attack or failure.
words.example: They fortified the town walls with extra stone before the enemy arrived.
words.mnemonic: fort + -ify: to turn something into a FORT, making it tough and defensible.

words.definition: Open disagreement with an official or widely held opinion.
words.example: A single justice voiced her dissent while the rest of the court lined up the other way.
words.mnemonic: dis- (apart) + sent (to feel, as in 'sentiment'): to feel APART from the crowd.

words.definition: Inclined to find trivial faults and raise petty objections.
words.example: Her captious editor flagged every stray comma but ignored the broken argument.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'capture' — always trying to capture your tiniest mistakes.

words.definition: Fond of arguing and quick to provoke or join a quarrel.
words.example: The disputatious student challenged nearly every claim the professor made.
words.mnemonic: dispute + -atious: describes a person whose very nature is to dispute everything.

words.definition: Stubbornly attached to a theory while ignoring practical realities or differing opinions.
words.example: The doctrinaire economist refused to revise his model even as the recession deepened.
words.mnemonic: doctrine + -aire: someone married to their doctrine, no matter what the facts say.

words.definition: Showing intense, heartfelt emotion or burning enthusiasm about something.
words.example: Her fervent support for the cause kept the exhausted volunteers going all night.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'fervor' and 'furnace' — feelings hot enough to boil.

words.definition: Stated fully and clearly, leaving no room for confusion or doubt.
words.example: The instructions were explicit, listing every step so no one could get lost.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out) + plicit (fold): fully unfolded and laid out in the open.

words.definition: So convincing or interesting that it forcibly holds your attention or belief.
words.example: The lawyer's compelling argument left every juror nodding in agreement.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'compel' — it forces you to pay attention or agree.

words.definition: To influence someone's opinion or nudge them toward a decision.
words.example: A single heartfelt speech can sway voters who arrived completely undecided.
words.mnemonic: Picture a hypnotist's pendulum swinging back and forth, swaying your mind.

words.definition: To gently and patiently persuade someone to do something.
words.example: She coaxed the frightened kitten out from under the porch with a trail of treats.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Cokes' — offer someone a Coke to gently win them over.

words.definition: To ask someone earnestly and anxiously for something.
words.example: The refugees entreated the officials to open the border before nightfall.
words.mnemonic: en- + treat: you plead with someone for kind treatment.

words.definition: To beg someone desperately and emotionally to do something.
words.example: He implored the judge for mercy, his voice cracking with desperation.
words.mnemonic: im- + plore ('cry out') — crying out urgently for help.

words.definition: To ask someone urgently and anxiously, often while pleading.
words.example: The villagers beseeched the king to spare their harvest from the new tax.
words.mnemonic: be- + seech ('seek'): to seek something desperately from another person.

words.definition: To pester someone with repeated, insistent, and often annoying requests.
words.example: Street vendors importuned every tourist who paused, tugging sleeves and shouting prices.
words.mnemonic: 'important' + 'tune' — someone nagging you with the same 'important' tune again and again.

words.definition: To formally ask someone for money, help, support, or business.
words.example: The charity volunteers solicited donations from shoppers outside the mall.
words.mnemonic: so-LICIT — asking for something in a licit (lawful) way.

words.definition: To publicly support or argue in favor of a cause or policy.
words.example: She advocates for cleaner rivers, speaking up at every town council meeting.
words.mnemonic: ad- + voc ('voice'): to add your voice on behalf of a cause.

words.definition: To fight for, defend, or actively support a person or cause.
words.example: The senator championed workers' rights long before it became popular.
words.mnemonic: A prize-fighting champion steps into the ring to battle on your behalf.

words.definition: To adopt and openly support a belief, cause, or way of life.
words.example: After years of doubt, he espoused vegetarianism and never looked back.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'spouse' — you marry yourself to an idea.

words.definition: To spread and promote an idea, belief, or information widely.
words.example: Social media let the rumor propagate across the country within hours.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'propaganda' — pushing a message far and wide.

words.definition: To spread information or ideas widely to many people.
words.example: The health ministry worked to disseminate accurate guidance before the flu season peaked.
words.mnemonic: dis-SEMINATE — like scattering seeds (Latin 'semen' = seed) across a whole field.

words.definition: To officially announce or put a new law or rule into effect.
words.example: The council promulgated the new zoning ordinance the morning after the vote.
words.mnemonic: PROMO + gate — picture a 'promo at the gate': officials publicly posting the new rule at the entrance.

words.definition: Only slightly related to the main subject; going off on a side point.
words.example: Her question was tangential, so the professor set it aside to keep the lecture on track.
words.mnemonic: Picture a tangent line touching a circle at just one point — barely connected to the rest.

words.definition: An argument or reply that opposes and tries to disprove a claim.
words.example: After the prosecutor finished, the defense offered a sharp rebuttal that dismantled the timeline.
words.mnemonic: RE-BUT — it's the moment you say 'but...' right back: 'but here's why you're wrong.'

words.definition: To loudly and angrily criticize or denounce something.
words.example: The senator fulminated against the tax bill for nearly an hour, pounding the podium.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'full' + 'detonate' — a full-blown verbal explosion (Latin 'fulmen' = thunderbolt).

words.definition: To speak or write with strong hostility against someone or something.
words.example: Columnists inveighed against the factory owners who ignored every safety warning.
words.mnemonic: in-VEIGH sounds like 'invade' — you verbally invade and attack a target with words.

words.definition: To agree to a request or demand, often after resistance.
words.example: Worn down by weeks of protest, management finally acceded to the workers' pay demands.
words.mnemonic: AC-CEDE — you 'cede' (give up) ground and finally say yes.

words.definition: To have the same opinion as someone else; to agree.
words.example: The three judges concurred, and the ruling was unanimous.
words.mnemonic: CON + CUR (Latin 'currere' = to run) — two minds running together toward the same view.

words.definition: To declare or provide evidence that something is true or genuine.
words.example: Three witnesses can attest that she was home the entire evening.
words.mnemonic: A-TEST — passing a test proves something is real, so you attest to it.

words.definition: To state firmly that something is true or to confirm a decision.
words.example: The appeals court affirmed the lower ruling, letting the verdict stand.
words.mnemonic: AF-FIRM — you say it firmly, standing firm behind your statement.

words.definition: The quality of being clear, logical, and highly convincing.
words.example: The lawyer's closing argument had such cogency that the jury deliberated only minutes.
words.mnemonic: Picture tight, meshing 'cogs' of logic — reasoning so well-geared it turns smoothly and convinces.

words.definition: To formally give up a claim, right, or belief.
words.example: He renounced his throne to marry a commoner, shocking the entire court.
words.mnemonic: The opposite of 'announce' owning something — you announce that you're done with it and let it go.

words.definition: To state a specific requirement as a condition of an agreement.
words.example: The lease stipulates that no pets are allowed without written permission.
words.mnemonic: STIP sounds like 'strip' — think of a strip of fine print spelling out the exact conditions.

words.definition: Very difficult to manage, control, or solve.
words.example: Decades later, the region's water shortage remains an intractable problem.
words.mnemonic: IN (not) + TRACTABLE (able to be pulled/led, like a 'tractor') — a mule that simply won't be pulled into line.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — argument and persuasion
